questions.q: Define electronegativity and state its trend across Period 3 from Na to Cl.
questions.a: Electronegativity is the ability of a bonded atom to attract the shared electron pair; it increases from Na to Cl across Period 3. A wrong answer that says electronegativity decreases across a period reveals confusion between atomic size trend (which decreases) and electronegativity trend, or misunderstanding that greater nuclear charge increases pull on bonding electrons.

questions.q: Why is Al₂O₃ amphoteric while Na₂O is basic and Cl₂O₇ is acidic? Explain using electronegativity and charge density.
questions.a: Al has intermediate electronegativity (1.61) and high charge density (Al³⁺ small size, +3 charge) so it polarises the O–H bond in Al(OH)₃ enough to donate H⁺ (acidic) but not so strongly that it cannot accept OH⁻ (basic). Na has low electronegativity (0.93) and low charge density (Na⁺ large, +1) so Na₂O forms strongly basic NaOH. Cl has high electronegativity (3.16) and forms covalent Cl₂O₇ which hydrolyses to strong acid HClO₄. A wrong answer that only cites "metallic character" without linking to electronegativity and charge density shows superficial memorisation without mechanistic understanding.

questions.q: Predict the nature of the oxide of an element X (atomic number 14) and write the balanced chemical equation for its reaction with (a) NaOH and (b) HF. Identify the products.
questions.a:
Element X is Si (Group 14, Period 3). SiO₂ is acidic (non-metal oxide).
(a) SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O (sodium silicate)
(b) SiO₂ + 4HF → SiF₄ + 2H₂O (silicon tetrafluoride gas)
A wrong answer writing SiO₂ + 2HCl → SiCl₄ + H₂O reveals the misconception that all acids react with acidic oxides; HF is needed because F⁻ forms strong Si–F bonds, while Cl⁻ does not. Missing the state of SiF₄ (gas) loses a mark in board exams.

questions.q: Compare the acidic strength of the hydrated oxides of Period 3 elements: Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂, Cl₂O₇. Arrange them in increasing order of acidic character and justify the trend using electronegativity and oxidation state.
questions.a: Increasing acidic character: Na₂O (strongly basic) < MgO (basic) < Al₂O₃ (amphoteric) < SiO₂ (weakly acidic) < P₄O₁₀ (acidic) < SO₂ (acidic) < Cl₂O₇ (strongly acidic). Justification: Electronegativity increases left to right, and oxidation state of the element in its highest oxide also increases (+1 to +7), both increasing polarisation of the O–H bond in the hydrated oxide, making H⁺ release easier. A wrong answer that ignores oxidation state (e.g., says SO₂ more acidic than P₄O₁₀ because S more electronegative than P) misses that P is +5 and S is +4 in these oxides; the combined effect decides acidity.

questions.q: A student writes: "CO is a neutral oxide because carbon has electronegativity 2.55 and oxygen 3.44, so the bond is non-polar." Evaluate this statement and correct it.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. CO has a polar covalent bond (ΔEN = 0.89), but it is neutral because it does not react with water to form an acid or base; it is not an acidic or basic anhydride. Neutral oxides (CO, N₂O, NO) have low oxidation states and do not hydrolyse. The student confuses bond polarity with oxide nature. A wrong answer that says "CO is acidic because C is less electronegative" shows misunderstanding that oxide nature depends on hydrolysis behaviour, not just electronegativity difference.

questions.q: Design a simple laboratory experiment to distinguish between three unlabelled solid oxides: MgO, Al₂O₃, and SO₃ (solid at low temperature). List reagents, observations, and conclusions.
questions.a:
Reagents: dilute HCl, dilute NaOH, water, pH paper.
Procedure:
1. Add water to each oxide, test pH of resulting mixture.
   - MgO: pH > 7 (basic, forms Mg(OH)₂ slightly soluble)
   - Al₂O₃: pH ≈ 7 (insoluble, no reaction)
   - SO₃: pH < 1 (vigorous reaction, forms H₂SO₄)
2. For the water-insoluble residue (Al₂O₃), add HCl → dissolves (forms AlCl₃); add NaOH → dissolves (forms NaAlO₂). MgO dissolves only in HCl. SO₃ already reacted.
Conclusion: MgO basic, Al₂O₃ amphoteric, SO₃ acidic.
A poor answer that only uses litmus paper on dry oxides fails because solid oxides don't change litmus; they must be tested in aqueous medium or with acid/base.
